Domestic Violence Protection Order Data in Colorado in 2024

Author

Andrew MacFarland (andrew.macfarland@cuanschutz.edu)

Published

October 21, 2026

Summary

This report provides an overview of Colorado’s Domestic Violence Protection Order (DVPO) cases in 2024. It is an exploratory analysis should not be considered final. It was QA’d by Rachel Johnson in September 2026. Please do not distribute.

A First Look at the Data

Let’s first take a look at the data, to give a sense of what we’re working with.

Here is an example of all the entries for a single case, C0392024C 000022. Note six entries for the temp order hearing, on different dates. If we use the earliest date for each event, the temp order is heard and granted on the same day. If we use the latest date for each event, the temp order is granted on 01/08, 220 days before the hearing on 08/15.

Case Types and Event Codes

In 2024, the following events were filed n times. Temporary and permanent hearings and orders are categorized as “Protection Order Domestic Abuse” and mandatory orders are categorized as “Domestic Violence”.

Records were filtered to include only events with a status of “Hearing Held” or “missing” status (which include orders granted and vacated). Events with other statuses were excluded, including cases that were continued by the court, continued by the parties, or ended because a party failed to appear, as well as dissolution-of-marriage/permanent-order hearings. These represent rescheduling, cancellations, or unrelated proceedings rather than the outcomes this analysis is tracking.

Additionally, duplicate event records were removed. This reduced counts of events by a variable amount, depending on event type. For example, the total count of Temporary Protection Order Hearings was reduced from 7,052 to 7,051 while the total count of Mandatory Protection Orders Granted was reduced from 9,194 to 8,373.

Case Pathway Analysis

Individual cases can be traced from the initial temporary order hearing through other events, or to points where those events fail to occur. All events occurred in 2024, so it is likely that some cases do not include events that occurred before or after 2024. For simplicity, the analysis does not include orders vacated.

From the data provided we are not able to determine which orders were given a hearing and then denied an order. We can only see that a hearing occurred and then either an order was granted or there is no record of an order being granted.

Note that these values do not line up with the values in the table above. With these values, only one incidence of a given event code is counted per case number. So in the table above, one case might have had multiple temporary order hearings (recorded as occuring on different dates or with some other differing value), but in the case pathway analysis below, that case is only counted once as having had a temporary order hearing.

Erratic or Negative Elapsed Time

In the case pathway analysis above, note that the minimum number of days passing between one event and another is negative between each available time point. To better understand these numbers, here is a breakdown of how many days passed between events in the case pathway. Negative numbers indicate that the “second” event occurred before the “first” event (e.g., the temporary protection order was recorded as being granted BEFORE the initial temporary protection order hearing). Zero values were removed from histogram plots to better visualize non-zero values, with the number of zero values removed noted in footnote of each plot.

There are enough strange numbers here to question the accuracy of the data. Negative numbers are clearly a data entry issue, but high positive number may either be data entry errors or that a temporary order was not effective in protecting someone in crisis. Most numbers should be zero, indicating that an order was granted the same day as a hearing.

Note, only the EARLIEST record for every given event is retained. If only the latest record for every given event is retained, the timing can look very different. For example, if we look at the timing between temporary order hearings and temporary orders granted and compare analyses where the earliest record is used versus the latest record is used, we see the following changes:

  • Average days between events goes from -0.2 to 1.3
  • Minimum days between events goes from -78.0 days to -220
  • Maximum days between events goes from 321.0 days to 259
  • Standard deviation of days between events goes from 8.4 to 16.3

Counties with erratic or inconsistent timing may benefit from outreach for data quality improvement.

Cases by County

Here are plots of the top 15 counties by dvpo case filings in 2024 (by count and by rate). Absent is Denver County, cases from which are not included in the data. These data include temp order hearings, temp orders granted, perm order hearings, and perm orders granted.

Data missingness could be a function of which courts are doing hearings (e.g., municipal doing hearings rather than state). There is also concern about undercounting: Denver has thousands of cases but is not represented here.

Converstion Rates

This plot summarizes the top 15 counties by conversion rate in 2024. These compare the percentage of cases per county that moved from a temporary hearing to a permanent hearing.

County Rates Compared to CBI Data

Here is the incidence rate per county from the data we obtained from state judicial (incidence of htro - initial temporary order hearing), compared to same-year rates of domestic violence incidence and victimization from CBI. Some counties are missing either judicial data or CBI data. In some counties judicial rates can vary widely from CBI rates, either higher or lower. It is unclear why this might be. Note that the judicial data included here is only for “Protection Order Domestic Abuse” cases that include a temporary order hearing. “Domestic Violence” cases where mandatory protection orders were issued are not included in the judicial data.
